newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - AK Steel sees pressure on steelmakers.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - AK Steel sees pressure on steelmakers.

text.p: The several million tons of new domestic steel capacity coming on-stream in the next two years will rattle U.S. steelmakers by pressuring prices, squeezing earnings -- and likely forcing some high-cost producers into bankruptcy filings, said Thomas Graham, chairman of AK Steel Holding Corp.

"I think there will be a shakedown among domestic producers...'97 and '98 are going to be very difficult years," Graham told Reuters in an interview. "We're going to have a traumatic period the next year or two."
Several million short tons of flat-rolled steel capacity, primarily in the hot-rolled sheet segment of the market, are due to come onstream within the next two years from upstart mini-mill producers.

Graham said there is "probably not" ample room in the domestic market for the additional capacity and as a result, prices will fall, steel earnings will be squeezed and some "weakly-capitalized" steel firms that he declined to name could be forced into creditor protection.
"Those weakly-capitalized companies who are unable to stand the gaff of a period of very low prices and profits are liable to end up in Chapter 11," he said.

Graham, 69, is retiring from AK Steel in January following a long and storied career in the U.S. steel industry. He ran USX Corp's U.S. Steel, the nation's largest steelmaker, from 1983-1991, a troubled period of industry downsizing.
He then went on to head the former Washington Steel Corp in 1991, turning the financially beleagured company around and orchestrating its sale to Lukens Inc in April 1992.
In June 1992, Graham took the top post at the former Armco Steel Co LP, a joint-venture, limited partnership steel company that was losing millions of dollars a year.

Graham recapitalized the firm and it became a publicly owned company in 1994, being renamed AK Steel. Since going public, AK Steel has consistently been the industry's most profitable and efficient integrated steelmaker.
While declining to be specific, Graham said he will continue to work and consider a number of options, which could include running another financially troubled steel firm.
"I can't just lay my tools down. I don't have any intention of doing that," he said. "What form that's going to take isn't totally clear right now."
With AK Steel as the exception, integrated steel earnings have disappointed Wall Street in recent months by being lackluster at a time when steel demand is strong.
Several industry analysts as well as steelmakers have blamed weak earnings on an erosion in steel pricing, but Graham said the problem lies in steelmakers not controlling costs.

"I don't think (weak earnings) have been on the price side. There's a popular notion on that, but I don't think that's where you find the solution," he said. "We're all selling the same product at roughly the same price. The big difference in profitability has to be on the cost side."
